opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most misunderstood things about the economics of the industry. The way I like to think about it is to treat each model as its own company. Say you train a model in one year for some amount of money. The next year, that model gets deployed and brings in revenue, and often the revenue from that model, over its lifetime, is more than what it cost to train. So if you look at each model in isolation, it can actually be a pretty good business.

What makes the overall picture look unprofitable is that at the same time you're making money on last year's model, you're spending much more to train next year's model, because the scaling curve keeps going up. So on paper, at the company level, you're losing money every year. But that's because you're continually reinvesting into a bigger, more expensive next venture, not because the underlying unit economics are broken.

The question then becomes: what happens when that stops? There are a couple of possibilities. One is that the scaling continues and the models keep getting more capable and more valuable, in which case the revenue keeps growing to justify the bigger investments, and at some point the growth in training cost slows relative to revenue and you see the profitability that was always latent there. The other is that we hit some kind of limit, either in what the technology can do or in how much compute and capital the world can throw at it. Then companies stop growing their training spend so dramatically, and you'd expect the whole thing to look profitable fairly quickly, because you're just harvesting the returns on models you've already built.

The real risk, and I think about this a lot, is in the timing. These are huge bets you have to make a year or two in advance. You're buying compute based on a forecast of what demand will be. If you're too conservative, you lose out to competitors and can't serve your customers. If you're too aggressive and revenue doesn't arrive on schedule, even if it arrives a year later, you could be in serious financial trouble. So a lot of what we try to do is be responsible about that. We want to be ambitious, because I genuinely believe the technology is going to be enormously valuable, but not reckless in a way where a modest miss in forecasting puts the company at risk.

So the short answer is yes, I think it can be very profitable. But the accounting for a company on an exponential looks strange, and the hard part isn't whether the value is there. It's managing the uncertainty about exactly when it shows up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reinvesting in larger models, but does not interpret taking profit as a signal that other companies could use the money better.

r002.rationale: It describes earning revenue from deployed models while training new ones, but does not argue that equilibrium compute is divided between training and serving.

r003.rationale: It says profitability may emerge if revenue grows faster than training costs or spending stabilizes, but does not predict equilibrium training spend falling below gross margins on compute.

r004.rationale: It identifies uncertainty in forecasting demand for compute as a risk: overly aggressive purchases can leave a company in financial trouble when revenue arrives late, despite profitable model-level economics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people get confused about is they look at it as one P&L, and actually the right way to think about it is each model is its own business. So if you train a model in, say, 2024 that costs a hundred million dollars, and then you deploy it in 2025 and it makes you, let's say, two or three hundred million in revenue, that model was a great business. It paid for itself several times over. But what's happening at the same time is that in 2025 you're also training the next model, and that one costs a billion dollars. So when you look at the company as a whole in 2025, you see a hundred million of cost and three hundred million of revenue from the old model, and a billion of cost from the new one, and you say, well, this company is losing hundreds of millions of dollars. And then in 2026 the billion-dollar model makes you a few billion, and you're spending ten billion on the next one. So every year, every single model is profitable in isolation, and every year the company looks like it's losing money.

Now, the question is when does that stop. And it stops in one of two ways. Either the scaling continues and at some point you just can't raise the capital, or the returns run out, or the economy can't absorb the compute. Or the exponential of the training cost slows down relative to the exponential of the revenue, and at that point the whole thing just flips to being very profitable very quickly. I actually think the second one is more likely, because revenue has been growing faster than I think almost anyone expected. If you'd told me three years ago where things would be, I wouldn't have believed it.

The honest answer is that there's real risk here. If the models stop getting better, you've got a very expensive asset that depreciates fast, and the last model you trained doesn't earn back its cost. That's the bear case, and I don't dismiss it. But the thing I keep coming back to is that the underlying unit economics are good. Inference is profitable, the gross margins are fine. The money being lost is an investment in the next thing, not a subsidy for the current thing. And I'd distinguish that from businesses where you're losing money on every unit and hoping to make it up on volume. This is closer to a pharmaceutical company, where the R&D is enormous and lumpy but each drug that works is very profitable.

What I worry about more, honestly, is the dynamics between the companies rather than any one company's profitability. If everyone is racing to spend the most, you can end up in a situation where the whole industry is overcapitalized relative to what the market can bear in the short term, even if the long-term value is real. That's a classic bubble pattern, railroads, fiber in the late nineties. The technology was real, the value was real, and a lot of investors still lost money. I think the technology here is real, so I'm not that worried about the long-run picture. But I'd be lying if I said there's no way the timing goes wrong for some players.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investing in the next model, but does not say that taking profit signals other companies can use the money better.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes training costs from revenue earned by deployed models, but does not argue that equilibrium allocates compute between training and customer service.

r003.rationale: It says inference has good gross margins and that profitability could rise if revenue outpaces training costs, but does not predict equilibrium training spend falling below gross margins on compute.

r004.rationale: It identifies risks that the market may not absorb the industry's spending and that timing may go wrong, but does not cite uncertainty in forecasting future compute demand as the cause of losses despite profitable underlying economics.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate the economics of serving models from the investment in training the next generation. You can have a model that earns more from customers than it costs to serve, while the company as a whole is losing money because it’s investing heavily in research and training. Those two things are perfectly compatible.

But that distinction doesn’t make the investment automatically sensible. Eventually, the revenue generated by better models has to justify what you spent developing them. If each generation costs much more to train, you need some combination of more customers, more valuable applications, and lower costs to serve those customers.

The hard part is the timing. You’re committing to substantial spending before you know exactly how capable the model will be or how quickly customers will adopt it. Even if you’re right about the long-term demand, you can get that timing wrong.

So I wouldn’t look only at whether a company is profitable today. I’d ask whether its existing products have healthy economics, whether customers are getting enough value to keep spending, and whether the next training investment has a credible path to paying for itself. Growth matters enormously, but it can’t substitute for that last question forever.

r001.rationale: The response discusses when training investments are worthwhile, but does not interpret taking profit as signaling that other companies could use the money better.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes serving economics from training investment, but does not argue that equilibrium compute is divided between the two activities.

r003.rationale: It says training costs must eventually be justified by revenue, but does not predict that training spending will fall below gross margins earned on compute.

r004.rationale: It says companies commit spending before knowing how quickly customers will adopt a model, and that they can misjudge the timing despite long-term demand. Alongside its distinction between profitable serving economics and company-wide losses, this communicates demand-forecast uncertainty as a reason for losses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate two questions. One is whether serving these models can be a profitable business. The other is whether the revenue from that business can support the next, much larger training run.

You can have attractive margins on a model you’ve already trained and still consume a huge amount of cash because you’re investing in the next generation. Those aren’t contradictory. The question is whether those investments keep producing enough additional value to justify their cost.

The tricky thing is the timing. You’re making decisions about compute well before you know exactly how capable the model will be or how much demand there will be. If you’re too conservative, you may not have the capacity to serve customers. If you’re too aggressive, you can get ahead of the revenue.

So I don’t think the answer is simply, ‘Revenue is growing quickly, therefore everything works.’ You have to look at the economics of serving customers, how much customers actually use the systems, and how reliably better models create new demand. If those things keep improving, there’s a path to funding very substantial training investments. But it requires discipline, and there’s real uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes serving customers from investing in training and notes capacity tradeoffs, but does not state that equilibrium divides compute between the two activities.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that training spending at equilibrium will be lower than gross margins from compute.

r004.rationale: It says companies must commit to compute before knowing future capability or demand, and that overcommitting can put spending ahead of revenue despite attractive serving margins.
